reasoning: The core problem — an imperfect LLM/oversight monitor's PPV/precision collapsing at low misbehavior base rates, with audit-budget consequences — is explicitly covered by published AI-safety work. "Combining Cost-Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety" (arXiv 2507.15886) names the "false positive paradox" and uses Bayes-factor (TP/FP) reasoning to allocate a limited audit budget at rare prevalence, and the AI control literature (Greenblatt et al. 2312.06942; Control Tax 2506.05296) already formalizes the audit threshold via TPR·base_rate + FPR·(1−base_rate) = budget and safety ∝ log(audit budget). Most decisively, "The Verification Tax" (arXiv 2604.12951) frames AI auditing through the very diagnostic-screening/base-rate lens this proposal proposes ("the base rate problem... is among the oldest results in statistics"; miscalibration as a rare 'disease') and proves verification cost diverges as errors become rare. The underlying Bayes/PPV-NPV-vs-prevalence math is textbook epidemiology and textbook ML class imbalance. What remains unexplored is only the specific expository packaging — importing sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV vocabulary, measuring a weak LLM judge's sens/spec once on a labeled benchmark, then analytically sweeping PPV across base rates with an audit-budget plot — which is a minor presentation gap rather than a new finding.

evidence.title: Combining Cost-Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety
evidence.summary: Uses the Bayes factor (likelihood ratio of true to false positives) to allocate a limited false-positive/audit budget, auditing highest-Bayes-factor regions first. Explicitly invokes the 'false positive paradox': when misaligned outputs are rare, false-positive volume explodes and precision is poor despite good accuracy — the proposal's central claim, already established.

evidence.title: The Verification Tax: Fundamental Limits of AI Auditing in the Rare-Error Regime
evidence.summary: Frames AI auditing explicitly through the diagnostic-screening/base-rate lens the proposal proposes, treating miscalibration as a rare 'disease' and citing the base-rate problem as one of the oldest results in statistics. Proves a minimax verification-cost lower bound that diverges as errors become rare — a stronger, formal version of 'a seemingly-accurate judge becomes near-useless at low base rates.'

evidence.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
evidence.summary: Foundational AI-control work formalizing the audit-budget tradeoff at low attack base rates: 'affordable suspiciousness threshold' set by TPR·base_rate + FPR·(1−base_rate) = audit fraction, with safety scaling roughly with log of audit budget. Directly captures the audit-budget / false-alarms-per-true-catch analysis the proposal would produce.

evidence.title: Control Tax: The Price of Keeping AI in Check
evidence.summary: Quantifies that, when misaligned outputs are rare, operational cost is dominated by human auditing of ~0.1% of actions and by false positives — the audit-budget implication the proposal aims to visualize.

evidence.title: Base rate fallacy / false positive paradox; precision collapse at low prevalence
evidence.summary: Establishes the textbook math the proposal relies on: for fixed sensitivity/specificity (TPR/FPR), PPV (precision) approaches zero as positive prevalence approaches zero. This is standard epidemiology and ML class-imbalance knowledge, so the analytical core is not new.

evidence.title: AutoMonitor-Bench: Evaluating the Reliability of LLM-Based Misbehavior Monitor
evidence.summary: Recent benchmark evaluating reliability of LLM-based misbehavior monitors, including base-rate and false-positive considerations — confirms empirical measurement of LLM-judge sensitivity/specificity on labeled good/bad outputs is an active, occupied area.
